newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Moon Festival brings only tears for HK family.
newsitem.headline: Moon Festival brings only tears for HK family.

text.p: The mid-autumn festival, a happy Chinese celebration when families gather amid colourful lanterns and stay up to watch the moon, has brought only tears for relatives and friends of drowned activist David Chan.

The 45-year-old media consultant was one of five who tied ropes to their bodies and leapt over the bow of a rusty tanker that served as their protest ship in the East China Sea, asserting China's right to a cluster of disputed islands claimed by Japan.
Dragged in the vessel's wake early on Thursday, Chan lost consciousness and never recovered.
Relatives and friends gathered at Chan's Hong Kong office were overwhelmed with grief after the news broke of his death on the eve of the Moon Festival. Reporters heard wailing from inside.
Chan's youngest sister, Lai-hung, put on a brave face and told the media that whatever Chan had done was out of love for the motherland, China, which takes over this British colony next year.
"I believe it was his way to express his patriotism towards China," she said calmly. "Of course, we wish that (his death) was not the reality. I can tell you that he is in my heart forever."
Asked whether her brother had done the right thing in jumping into the water, Lai-hung said she could not pass judgment.
"I think I should be fair to him for whatever he had decided," she said. "I should respect his decision."
Chan's wife, Shun-hing, was not immediately available for comment.

The whole family was supportive of his mission to the disputed archipelago, which China refers to as the Diaoyu isles and Japan calls the Senkakus, and where Japanese rightists have built a lighthouse and raised Japanese flags.
Lai-hung refused to blame the Japanese for her brother's death, but a friend and fellow activist, Andy Tse, did not have any kind words for Tokyo.

"It was because there were so many Japanese ships there blocking our plan to land on the islands," Tse said. "Since we cannot get near, they went into the water to demonstrate China's claim of sovereignty."
The group of 18 Hong Kong activists had planned to assert Chinese sovereignty rights by raising a Chinese red flag on the disputed isles but were blocked by Japanese coast guard vessels.
Japan has claimed sovereignty over the islands and refused to acknowledge that the dispute is open for discussion.
Tokyo's claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
Hong Kong's government appealed for calm, and Governor Chris Patten said he was saddened by the drowning.
"This has been distressing for us, and I appeal for calm from all," Home Affairs Secretary Michael Suen told reporters when news of Chan's death broke.
"I urge the community to react to this development in...an orderly and responsible manner," Suen said.
Chan was survived by his wife, Shun-hing, an eight-year-old son and a 10-year-old daughter.
